text: Artifact creatures, Spacecraft, counters and the eight-power attackers. White has the weakest commons in the set (they average 53.0, the lowest of any colour) and its uncommons are not much better. The rares are another story: the white mythics and the double-strike artifact rare are among the best cards in the set.
Three of its four pairs sit near the bottom by deck win rate. RW is the exception, because red carries it. White is a colour to end up in for a strong rare, not one to aim for.

Spacecraft, dilemmas, bounce and card draw. Blue's commons are middling and its uncommons are flat (the reviewers graded nearly all of them between D+ and B-), with one standout, the expensive Strange New Worlds spell that draws and makes two bodies. The best common is the five-mana artifact that bounces a creature.

No common blue card kills anything; blue removal taps, stuns, bounces or puts a creature on top of the library. The reviewers liked blue commons more than the data does. UR and GU are the blue pairs that win; UB is the worst deck in the format.

Klingons, artifact creatures, dilemmas and the graveyard. Black has the most reliable removal (an unconditional instant at common, a cheap -2/-2 that grows when you sacrifice, a two-mana kill spell at uncommon) but the weakest uncommons of any colour, 52.4 on average. Several of them are dilemma payoffs, and those lose.
The rares are good, and the black pairs split sharply: BR and BG are top-three decks, while WB and UB are at the bottom.

Klingons, landfall and the eight-power attackers. Red is the best colour in the early data: the best commons (57.2 on average), the best uncommons (57.6) and the most removal, with burn at one, two, three and five mana and an X spell at uncommon.

This is the biggest gap between the reviewers and the data. Both reviewers and Draftsim called red's commons weak or flat. So far they are the best in the set, and several of them still go late (see Sleepers). All four red pairs have above-average deck win rates.

Landfall, Strange New Worlds, counters and self-mill. Green has the deepest rares by far (the seven green rares average 62.3), solid commons and good uncommons. Its common bite spell is the best common removal, and its two-drop mana creature fixes for any colour.
Green splits in two: half its commons feed the slow GU and BG decks (mill, lands, value), the other half the RG and GW attackers. RG is the best deck in the format and BG is third.

archetypes.name: Spacecraft tempo

text: Tempo and enters-the-battlefield value with a few Spacecraft on top. The signpost protects your Spacecraft and loots whenever it taps, which stationing does. Below average by deck win rate, mostly because white's commons are thin.
Don't overload on ships. Two or three good ones is the number both reviewers give; each one needs creatures to tap, and a deck with too many ends up tapping its blockers for nothing.

key: Hemmer, Fixing What Is Broken
Loots every time it taps to station. Spacecraft get hexproof on your turn.
Constable Odo
Locks down a creature for two turns or makes two Clues.
U.S.S. Excelsior, Cutting Edge
Kills a tapped creature on entry, then becomes a flyer.

archetypes.name: Dilemmas

text: Modal spells and creatures (any card that says choose one counts as facing a dilemma) with payoffs that draw, drain or grow when you choose. The worst deck in the format by a distance, under 50% in the early data.

The plan has plenty of enablers and almost no reward. The dilemma payoffs are among the weakest cards in the set, so the reviewers' advice holds: play the good modal cards for what they do and don't go all in. A UB deck built on black removal and blue tempo cards does better than one built on dilemmas.

key: Seven of Nine
The dilemma payoff. Draws a card per choice, but wins only about 50%.
Lore, Positronic Provocateur
Cheap hybrid body with a modal enter trigger.

archetypes.name: Klingon aggro

text: Klingons, hasty 2/1 tokens and sacrifice. Not quite all-out aggro: the deck does a little more each turn, makes tokens that die anyway and turns them into value. Second best by deck win rate, and the gold cards are very good.
Most of the set's Klingons are here, so the Klingon tricks and payoffs work. Red supplies the burn and black the kill spells, which makes it the pair with the most removal.

key: The Duras Sisters
A hybrid two-drop that leaves a hasty token behind. The best gold uncommon.
L'Rell, Fierce Visionary
A hasty attacker every turn, plus a sacrifice outlet.
Gowron, Eager for Battle
Grows when anything dies and draws off sacrificed Klingons.

archetypes.name: Landfall stompy

text: Put as many stats on the board as fast as you can and trigger landfall on the way. The best deck in the format so far, at 59.2.

Landfall creatures are weak as late draws, so play them on curve while you still have land drops. Extra land drops, Planet tokens made at instant speed and the green land searchers give second triggers in a turn. Hasty and trampling threats let the deck finish games before the slower decks take over.

theme.label: landfall
enabler: basic land card or Planet card

key: Dal R'El, Augment Orphan
Ramps on every land drop and turns spare lands into cards.
Hit It!
Haste for the team and a land off the top.
Cleveland Booker, Empath
A 2/2 token on every land drop.

archetypes.name: Counters

text: +1/+1 counters, Doctors and a wide board, with payoffs that draw cards or spread more counters. The reviewers suggested it for newer players. The early data disagree: it is one of the three weakest pairs, and both gold counter payoffs win under 51%.
Green's good commons still make it playable. Treat the counters as a bonus on cards that are good anyway and don't take the gold payoffs early.

key: Phlox, Unorthodox Doctor
Draws whenever a creature with a counter connects. Loses in the early data.
The Doctor, EMH
Spreads counters across the team. Also below average so far.

archetypes.name: Borg artifacts

text: Artifact creatures, Borg and lords that pump them. Both reviewers named it a likely top deck and the sealed guide called it pretty strong. The early data rank it ninth of ten, at 53.1.

The gold cards and the rares are good; the problem is the commons that fill the deck, which are among the weakest in white and black. It needs a lot of artifact creatures to make the payoffs work, around 14 or 15 in a 17-creature deck by the reviewers' count. Pick it up when the double-strike rare or the lord comes, not before.

key: Locutus, the One Who Speaks
Lord for artifact creatures, or a removal spell from your hand.
Zero, Incorporeal Sensate
Hybrid lifelinker that taxes their best card.
Primary Unimatrix Adjunct
Double strike for every artifact creature. The reason to be here.

archetypes.name: Spells tempo

text: Cheap creatures, instants and sorceries, and payoffs that care about noncreature spells. Above average at 56.0. The signpost two-drop is one of the best gold cards and wins even more for strong players.
It wants about ten noncreature spells for the signpost to hit reliably; eight is playable, fewer is not. Red's burn does most of the work, and blue's bounce and counters keep the tempo.

key: Spock, Always Your Friend
Finds a spell from the top four. A top uncommon.
Gray and Adira, Forever Joined
Copies a creature each turn you cast a spell. Weaker than it looks.

archetypes.name: Graveyard value

text: Mill, surveil and bring cards back, with payoffs that trigger when a card leaves your graveyard. Third by deck win rate, and BG cards do better here than anywhere else: the average card wins over two points more in BG than its overall rate.
A grindy deck. Make good trades, don't race, and let the value creatures and black removal take over. Milled cards with beam me up are free spells, which is why the reviewers liked the overlap.

key: Nog, Ambitious Cadet
A two-drop that levels into a 3/4 that surveils.
Vash, Freelance Archaeologist
Surveils every turn and draws when a card leaves the graveyard.
Daniels, Temporal Agent
Brings back a creature card, then recycles itself.

archetypes.name: Eight power

text: Play a creature every turn and attack with eight or more total power to switch on the payoffs. Fourth by deck win rate, and it has the best common in the set, a red three-drop that pumps an attacker every combat.

Eight power is less than it sounds: a two-drop, a three-drop and most four-drops get there. The catch is that trades drop you below it again, so the deck wants more bodies, not tricks. Equipment adds power to one creature only.

key: Kirk, Commanding Officer
Card advantage on every attack with eight power.
Worf, Honor-Bound Warrior
Hybrid two-drop that doubles its power.
Cantankerous Captain
The best common in the set. Gives menace once you reach eight power.

archetypes.name: Strange New Worlds

text: Count differently named lands: Planet duals at common, shock lands at rare, the colourless Anomaly lands and New Planet tokens. Payoffs get cheaper or bigger with each name. Just below the middle by deck win rate, and the most played deck on Arena in the first days according to the reviewers.

A two-colour deck with a dual and a colourless land gets to about three names, the floor. Draft fixing highly here: four to seven tapped duals is fine in this deck, though not in others. The reviewers also note a mill plan with the blue card that takes their top land.

key: The Traveler
Power equals your land names. A top gold uncommon.
Cloak and Phaser
Two bodies and two cards, cheaper with each land name.
Earth, Sector 001
The GU Planet dual. The best of the common lands.

text: Star Trek is a Universes Beyond set with crews, starships and planets. Each two-colour pair has its own plan, from Klingon aggro to counting differently named lands. Most decks play cheap creatures with enter-the-battlefield effects, and beam me up lets you cast cards from the graveyard by picking one of those creatures back up.

This is an early guide. The numbers come from the first four days of 17Lands Premier Draft data (about 64,000 games, 9,000 of them from strong players), so rare and mythic win rates are rough and the deck-level numbers that the Bloomburrow guide has are not out yet. The card reviews come from a two-host set review podcast, a sealed guide and Draftsim's set review. When they disagree with the data, the page says so. Where the guide says strong players, it means 17Lands users who win 60% or more of their games.

sections.heading: The format in short
list: Red and green are the deep colours. Red has the best commons and uncommons so far and the most removal; green has the best rares.
RG, BR, BG and RW have the best deck win rates. UB is clearly the worst, and WB, GW and WU are close behind it.
Removal is narrower than usual: most of it is damage, size-limited or sorcery speed. Take the clean answers when you see them.
Beam me up rewards cheap creatures with good enter effects. Pick up a one- or two-drop to recast the spell, never your five-drop.
Spacecraft are good in twos and threes, not tens. They need creatures to tap.
Not every theme pays off. Klingons, landfall, the graveyard and land names work. Dilemmas, the counters payoffs and the Mission enchantments lose.
Rares matter a lot: ten of them win at 63.8 or more, against 60.8 for the best common.
The ten common Planet duals are solid and go late. Most decks want one or two; GU wants as many as it can get.

text: Early picks: power first, then removal. The green, white and red rares at the top of the set come first whatever their colour, then clean removal (red burn, black kill spells, the green bite spell), then the best gold uncommons. A strong gold two-drop is a fine early pick, but it ties you to two colours on pick one.

sections.heading: Lean toward red
text: Red is the best colour in the early data, and the table hasn't caught up. Reviewers called red's commons flat or weak, and drafters take them that way: the best common in the set is often still there at pick six or seven, and a red aura that wins almost as much goes even later. If red keeps flowing in pack 1, take the hint.
Green is the other deep colour. Its rares are the best in the set, and it pairs best with red and black.

sections.heading: Which themes are worth it
text: Some plans in this set pay off and some don't, and you can't tell from the card text. The ones that work: Klingons and sacrifice in BR, landfall in RG, graveyard value in BG, eight power in RW and land names in GU. Their gold cards are good and their commons hold up.

The ones that don't, so far: dilemmas in UB, counters in GW and artifact creatures in WB. In each case the enablers are fine cards but the payoffs lose, and the decks rank near the bottom. You can still end up in those colours. Just draft them as good cards plus removal, and don't take the payoff early hoping the theme comes.
Sharing a mechanic isn't support. A card that rewards you for land names needs real land names; a card that rewards Klingons needs Klingons.

sections.heading: Lands
text: The common Planet duals (tapped, gain one life, two colours) win about as often as an average card and still go late. In a normal two-colour deck take two of yours: better mana without too many slow turns. In GU take every one you can, because each one is another land name.
The colourless Anomaly lands that sacrifice for an effect are a real cost to your coloured mana. Play one at most. The rare shock lands are fine but not worth a high pick outside GU.

sections.heading: Main colour and second colour
text: This held in Bloomburrow's draft data and is general enough to carry over; TRK's draft data isn't public yet. You don't draft two colours at once. Pack 1 settles one colour, and the second gets decided in pack 2 once you see what the table is leaving alone.

Count as you go. A finished deck is about 13 cards of the main colour and 8 of the second. Once the main colour has about seven good cards, another average one only pushes out your weakest. A decent card in the colour you are short of adds one.

sections.heading: Reading what is open
text: In packs 1 and 3 the same neighbour passes to you; in pack 2 it is the other one. So what you see late in pack 1 tells you about pack 3. A signal is a good card arriving later than it normally gets taken. In this set, the late red commons are a signal only if they are later than usual, because everyone is passing them a bit.

sections.heading: Where people go wrong
text: Flashy rares with weak results get taken in the first three picks (see Traps). The dilemma payoffs, the Mission enchantments and the counters gold cards look like build-arounds and play like filler. The Sleepers page lists cards that win more than their pick order suggests.

17Lands hasn't published TRK's game data yet, so this page can't give the measured deck numbers the Bloomburrow guide has (land count, creature count, curve by result). What follows is the reviewers' advice plus what the card data already show. Expect this page to change.

sections.heading: The shape
list: Two colours. There are no over-the-top bombs worth bending the mana for, so splash only a strong single-pip rare or removal spell, and only with a dual or a green fixer.
Keep the curve low and affect the board early. Both reviewers expect pressure from cheap creatures, more than in the last set, and a good one-drop is worth more than usual.
Plenty of creatures. Spacecraft, beam me up and the eight-power cards all need bodies.
Two or three Spacecraft at most, and only the good ones.
Count beam me up cards as half a card more: you will cast the good ones twice. Pick up cheap creatures to do it.

sections.heading: Lands
text: The reviewers build with 17 lands. Take two Planet duals for your colours in a normal deck; GU can play four to seven. Play at most one colourless Anomaly land, ideally as a seventeenth or eighteenth land when you can't cut a basic.
Land cyclers are weaker here than in recent sets: the bodies are big but plain, and there is little to reanimate them with.

sections.heading: Removal
text: Removal in this set is mostly damage, a size condition or sorcery speed, so plan what each spell can kill. Black's -X/-X and the four-power condition on the white common both have awkward gaps. Take a solid removal spell over a pretty good creature: the reviewers felt the shortage, and the data back them, since nearly all the clean removal wins above average.

sections.heading: Cards to leave out
text: The Mission enchantments are too slow for what they give. Both reviewers said so and all of them lose in the data. The Test sorceries and instants are mostly weak too; the least bad is red's Klingon one, in BR. Stun and tap removal is worse than it looks against beam me up decks, which happily pick the stunned creature back up.

pages.title: Beam me up
pages.summary: Cast the card again from your graveyard by also returning a creature you control to your hand
pages.verdict: Good with cheap enter-the-battlefield creatures. The best ones are spells you want twice.

text: Beam me up works like flashback with an extra cost: return a creature you control to its owner's hand. That is a downside unless the creature does something when it enters, and in this set many do. Pick up a one- or two-drop and replay it; never return the five-drop. It is sorcery speed, so it can't save a creature from removal. Milling or discarding these cards is free value, which is why the graveyard decks like them.
The reviewers expected it to define the format. The data mostly agree for the burn and token spells and disagree for the white ones.
cards: Three damage twice. The best beam me up card.
A hasty token now and another later.
Counters twice still isn't enough. One of the weakest commons.

pages.title: Spacecraft
pages.summary: Artifacts you charge by tapping creatures (station); at enough counters they become flying creatures
pages.verdict: Play two or three good ones. More than that and they stop working.

text: To station, tap another creature you control as a sorcery and put charge counters equal to its power on the Spacecraft. At the number on the card (often six) it becomes an artifact creature, and most fly. Thresholds are lower than in the last set with Spacecraft. Most of the set's flying is on these ships, so a charged one gets in.

They need a fair creature count. A deck full of ships taps its blockers for nothing. The ones that come with a body or an enter effect play best. Against a loaded ship, a tap or stun effect at instant speed is a big tempo swing.
cards: The best card in the set by win rate. Casts a free spell on entry and every attack.
A two-mana ship that fetches a land. Solid filler for white.
Stuns on entry, then asks a lot. Below average.

pages.title: Strange New Worlds
pages.summary: Gets cheaper or bigger with each differently named land you control
pages.verdict: GU's mechanic. Strong payoffs that need real land variety.

text: It counts land names, not colours or types: two copies of the same dual count once, but every basic type, Planet dual, shock land, Anomaly land and New Planet token adds one. A plain two-colour deck with one dual reaches three, which is the floor. GU decks with several duals reach four to seven by the mid game, and the payoffs get very good there.
cards: Grows with land names and lets you play lands off the top.
The best blue uncommon. Cast it for about five mana.
A repeatable tapper that is too slow for most decks.

pages.title: Dilemmas
pages.summary: You face a dilemma whenever you choose a mode for a spell or ability
pages.verdict: Lots of enablers, weak payoffs. Play modal cards for what they do.

text: Every choose-one card, and every ability that asks you to choose, counts as facing a dilemma. The set is full of them, so any deck faces a few. The payoffs are what make it a plan: cards that draw, drain, grow or return when you choose. They are mostly in blue and black.

Those payoffs are among the worst cards in the set so far, and UB, the dilemma pair, is the worst deck. The reviewers saw it coming and warned against going all in. Modal cards are good because both modes are often worth a card, not because of the payoffs.
cards: A soft counter or a stun and a card. One of the better blue commons.
The weakest card in the set.

pages.title: Landfall
pages.summary: Triggers whenever a land enters under your control
pages.verdict: RG's mechanic, and the best deck. Play landfall cards on curve.

text: Landfall cards trigger on every land drop, so they are strong early and weak as late top-decks. Extra land drops, instant-speed Planet tokens and the green cards that put lands onto the battlefield give a second trigger in a turn. Most payoffs are red and green.
cards: A two-drop that hits hard on land turns. Goes late for how good it is.
Card advantage off land drops, but slow. One of the weaker Missions.

pages.title: Eight power
pages.summary: Bonuses when you attack while your creatures have total power 8 or more
pages.verdict: RW's mechanic. Easier to reach than it sounds; trades take it away.

text: Attack with eight or more total power on your side of the table and these cards switch on: extra cards, double power, menace, can't-block effects. A two-drop, a three-drop and a four-drop usually get there. Trades and removal knock you back below, so the deck wants a creature every turn rather than tricks. The red commons that use it are some of the best in the set.
cards: The best common in the set.
Stops a blocker on every big attack.
Cheap but below average so far.

pages.title: Borg and artifact creatures
pages.summary: Lords and engines that reward a board of artifact creatures
pages.verdict: WB's plan. Great rares, weak commons. Needs a lot of artifact creatures.

text: Many creatures in this set are artifacts, and the Borg are WB's version of a tribe. The payoffs pump, draw or copy across all your artifact creatures, so they need a board of them: the reviewers count 14 or 15 in a 17-creature deck. Borg don't count for Federation.
The rare payoffs are excellent. The common and uncommon Borg are not, which is why WB sits near the bottom despite the hype.
cards: Double strike for the team. A bomb in the right deck.
Makes a Borg token on every hit.
Only as big as your artifact creature count. Weak.

pages.title: Federation
pages.summary: Counts the creature types among your non-Borg creatures
pages.verdict: Easy to misread. Only a few cards below rare.

text: Federation counts creature types, not creatures: a Human Officer counts two, and a second Human Officer adds nothing. Borg don't count. With the set's many types, four or five is normal by the mid game. It appears on only a handful of cards below rare.
cards: A rare that turns Federation into a big pump every turn.
Flash removal that is often too small. Below average.

pages.title: Missions
pages.summary: Uncommon enchantments that collect quest counters for a bigger effect
pages.verdict: A trap cycle. All of them lose.

text: Each Mission asks you to do something (cast noncreature spells, play creatures, have creatures die), gives a small effect each time and a bigger one at a set number of counters. They are too slow for what they give, and the reviewers, Draftsim and the data all agree. Three of them are among the ten weakest cards in the set.

pages.title: Planets and lands
pages.summary: Common tapped duals named after planets, New Planet tokens and land-searching cards
pages.verdict: Better than they look. Two in most decks, many more in GU.

text: The ten common Planets are tapped duals that gain a life. They win about average and still go late: the GU one is among the best commons in the set. Several cards make a New Planet token, a tapped land that taps for any colour, and the green land searchers can find Planets as well as basics. Every Planet is another land name for Strange New Worlds and another landfall trigger for RG.
cards: The GU dual. The best of the common lands.
The red Anomaly land: removal in your land slot.

text: The cards that take over a game, all rares and mythics. Most of them have only 500 to 1,300 games behind them so far, so the exact order will move. Green has the most.
cards: A free spell when it enters and on every attack. The best card in the set so far.
A wave of tokens, then counters whenever your creatures die.
A two-drop that grows and ramps every turn.
Value on entry and every attack, and more with an empty hand.
A lord that makes a token with every creature you cast.
Every creature explores. Card and land advantage in one.
Two 3/3s for four mana, and every later token becomes a 3/3.
Will Riker, First in the Field
Two temporary lands every turn: extra mana and two landfall triggers.
Double strike for every artifact creature.
A cheap body that grows and turns lands off the top into card advantage.

sections.heading: Just below
text: Removal and value rares that also win very often.
cards: Four damage, then you steal the creature for a turn.
Two bodies and a big pump every turn.

text: Removal is narrower than usual: damage, size conditions, sorcery speed. Red has the most of it and black the cleanest. Best first, by early win rate and how cleanly it answers a creature.
cards: Rare. Four damage and a stolen attacker.
Three damage, and again from the graveyard.
Bite with one or two creatures. The best common removal.
A fight, three life and a creature back.
Three damage at instant speed, with a loot.
One mana for two damage, four if something died.
An edict or a small sweeper on a body.
Two-mana kill spell for anything but an artifact creature.
Unconditional instant. The cleanest common removal.
Exiles any nonland permanent and has ward.
A cheap -2/-2, or -6/-6 if you sacrifice something.
Bounce on a body. The best blue common.
Six damage, and your land becomes a Planet.

sections.heading: Weaker than it looks
text: Removal that the reviewers or Draftsim rated highly and the data don't. The white exile spell hands them a land and wins under 51%.
cards: Clean exile, but the land it gives back costs you.
The kill mode gives them two tokens.

text: Cards that do worse than their rarity or pick order suggests. These are the weakest commons and uncommons so far:
cards: The worst card in the set.
A dilemma payoff that doesn't pay.
